newsitem.title: CHINA: INTERVIEW-HK pulls out stops to meet housing target.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-HK pulls out stops to meet housing target.

text.p: Hong Kong Secretary for Housing Dominic Wong said on Friday the government would pull out all stops to reach its housing supply target of 85,000 units a year and was determined to keep speculators out of the market.
"Our determination is very clear that we must build 85,000 flats a year with all that is available. Nothing must stand in the way," he told Reuters in an interview.
Hong Kong suffers from an acute shortage of housing.
Prices in the real estate market rose about 30 percent in the first half of the year before the government stepped in and vowed to increase the supply of new housing.
Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa set an annual target of 85,000 units, which Wong said could be achieved by 2001. "Beyond that we should be able to build no less than 85,000."
He said 36,000 units of the total target of 85,000 would come from the private sector. Private sector supply was expected to reach 22,000 units this year and 36,000 in 1998, he said.
To reach its housing goals, the government announced a five-year land sales programme last month, boosting residential land supply by 140 percent compared with the previous five years.
Wong said the government would simplify approval procedures for property developers. "We don't want red tape. We just want to cut out all the little things that are in the way," he said.

The amount of time needed to get approval for land rezoning, redevelopment and conversion would be reduced and the Housing Branch was working with the Secretary for Planning, Environment and Lands on plot ratio constraints. "We are working together to see how the development density of sites can be improved."
Wong said the government was also "thinking very seriously" about compulsory acquisition powers for the developers.
Asked whether the government was considering a scheme for the importation of labour, Wong said: "I do have a great interest in this matter."

"As far as I am concerned, we have announced plans for disposing of so much land and for building 85,000 flats per year. We therefore need whatever construction workers on the ground, including professionals, to deliver these targets."

While the government has launched a heavy public works programme, which should make some areas in the territory more accessible, he said some infrastructure development could be entrusted to the private sector to speed up the process.
"I certainly agree that while the government does not have the capacity to handle certain infrastructure works, then they could be entrusted to the private sector," he said.
"We will have to look at it on a project by project basis."
Property prices have slipped about five percent since Tung announced on July 1 his plans to increase housing supply and launch measures against property speculators if necessary.
"I am of course happy with the market's reaction that there is no sharp rise in prices and there are no outright speculative activities," said Wong.

He said the real estate market was currently dominated by end-users and he saw no current need to impose measures against property speculators. But he said the government continued to monitor the property market and did not rule out future action.
"Here I am dispelling some of the wrong statements that some people in the market seemed to have put out that the government are not doing anything. That is wrong," he said.
"The situation has not got to a point that we will do it but it does not mean that we will not do it," said Wong.
Tung is expected to release more details concerning the government's housing plans in a policy statement in October.
"We are now working out the details for the chief executive to elaborate in his policy address," said Wong.
